implemented: NFR-DR-S-001 maxPartBytes (per-part body cap): src/parse-multipart-related.ts wraps each per-part body Readable in a counting PassThrough when opts.maxPartBytes is set. The PassThrough is fed via an explicit 'data'/'end'/'error' bridge from dicer's per-part Readable (NOT via partStream.pipe) so the byte counter runs in-line with the listener-emit loop without racing the consumer's own listener attach. On overflow the counter destroys the upstream partStream, pushes MultipartPartTooLargeError({maxPartBytes,partIndex,bytesReceived}) into the queue, then ends the public counter cleanly so the consumer's drain on `body` resolves naturally — without this, the consumer would see 'Premature close' before our typed error surfaces. Default: undefined (no cap).

NFR-DR-S-012 maxParts (envelope-level cap): Layer A increments partsObserved on every dicer 'part' emit and trips when count > cap. On overflow, the offending partStream is destroyed and MultipartTooManyPartsError({maxParts,observed}) is pushed into the queue. observed === maxParts + 1 on first overflow. Default: 10_000 when undefined.

NFR-DR-S-004 maxHeadersPerPart + maxHeaderBytesPerPart: per-part 'header' event listener inspects the raw DicerHeaderBag, counts headers (sum of repeats per name) and sums header byte length using the framing formula `len(name) + 4 (": " + "\r\n") + len(value)` per repeat. measureHeaderValueBytes recurses through array shapes (dicer 0.3.1 emits string[]; the ambient shim documents Buffer/Buffer[]/Buffer[][] for forward-compat). On overflow, partStream.destroy() + queue.signalError(MultipartHeadersTooLargeError({limit,partIndex,cap,observed})). Defaults: maxHeadersPerPart=100, maxHeaderBytesPerPart=16_384.

NFR-DR-S-002 streamToString/streamToBuffer maxBytes: src/stream-helpers.ts gains a third positional `options` arg on streamToString and a second positional `options` arg on streamToBuffer. The exposed `StreamCollectOptions` interface holds `maxBytes?: number | undefined`. On overflow (`total > cap` strict-greater check), the cleanup function is called, source is destroyed, and the promise rejects with a generic Error per spec/api.md §3-4. Cap-undefined path is byte-identical to Sprint 1's helpers (backward-compat).

Behavior shift documented in JSDoc: callers omitting the fields previously saw no cap; from Sprint 6 onward, the 3 NFRs above default to safe values.

assumptions.context: Cap default values: maxParts=10_000, maxHeadersPerPart=100, maxHeaderBytesPerPart=16_384, maxPartBytes=undefined (no cap)
assumptions.choice: Per the planner's technicalNotes table and review-security.md F-S-001/004/012 recommendations. The defaults are applied via `?? <DEFAULT>` at validation-time so the values are fixed for the operation's lifetime (no race on opts mutation). maxPartBytes intentionally has no default because it's a per-part concern that depends on the application — the spec only mandates defaults for the 3 NFRs that target attacker-bombed envelopes.
alternatives_considered: Apply defaults inside the listener handlers (rejected — would re-resolve every fire and risk inconsistency if opts was mutated mid-stream)
Set defaults as named constants in a single CAPS_DEFAULTS object (rejected — three values are easy to inline-read at the validation site; a constants block adds indirection)

Force callers to opt-in by requiring `maxParts:10_000` literally in every call (rejected — the spec recommends defaults; making them explicit is a behavior shift from Sprint 1-5 where omitted == no cap, but it's the right shift per the security review)

assumptions.choice: Charge `Buffer.byteLength(name) + 4 + measureHeaderValueBytes(value)` per logical header line. The `+ 4` is `": "` (2 bytes) + `"\r\n"` (2 bytes) — the on-the-wire framing per RFC 7230 §3.2. For a header name with N repeated values, charge N × (nameBytes + 4) + sum(value bytes). The cap is SOFT (under-count is safe; over-count would false-positive); using a deterministic on-the-wire approximation is the right shape.
alternatives_considered: Charge only the value bytes, no framing (rejected — would under-count by ~10-20% on small headers, weakening the cap)

Use rawHeaders (Buffer.alloc(0) currently — Sprint 2 carry-over) and measure the actual byte block dicer captured (rejected — rawHeaders isn't populated by dicer 0.3.1's emit shape we're using; reconstructing it would require interception of dicer's internal HeaderParser which is out of scope)
Reuse flattenDicerHeaders + Buffer.byteLength on the joined string (rejected — the flatten step joins repeats with `, ` per RFC 7230, which doesn't match the on-the-wire framing per repeat)

assumptions.context: maxPartBytes implementation strategy: counting PassThrough wrapper vs. direct 'data' listener on partStream
assumptions.choice: Counting PassThrough wrapper. Initial implementation tried attaching a 'data' listener directly to dicer's per-part Readable; the test for the cap-forwarding case (Sprint 5's existing fetch-and-handle.test.ts) timed out because attaching the listener put partStream into flowing mode BEFORE the consumer's `streamToString` could attach its own 'data' listener (race window: dicer pumps body bytes synchronously after the 'header' emit; the consumer's parser microtask doesn't run until after the queue.push resolver's continuation, by which time chunks may have flowed past). The PassThrough approach: bridge partStream's 'data'/'end'/'error' through to a counter PassThrough that we expose as `body`. The PassThrough buffers writes when downstream isn't reading, so the consumer's later listener attach catches every byte. On overflow, we destroy partStream, push the typed error, and end the counter cleanly so the consumer's drain resolves naturally (NOT destroy — destroying the counter mid-drain surfaces 'Premature close' before our typed error has a chance to surface from the iterator's next .next()).
alternatives_considered: partStream.pipe(counter) + 'data' listener on partStream (rejected — the EventEmitter snapshot race: 'data' listeners are snapshotted at the start of emit(); when our counter listener trips and unpipes, the pipe's data callback (already in the snapshot) still fires for the current chunk and writes to the now-ended counter, surfacing 'write after end')
Direct 'data' listener on partStream (rejected — race with consumer listener attach, see above)
Use Node's `stream.Transform` with `_transform` (rejected — same buffering semantics as PassThrough, but with extra ceremony for the byte counting; PassThrough is the canonical idiom)
Schedule cap-check on setImmediate after queue.push (rejected — adds a tick of latency between trip and cleanup; the PassThrough approach gives synchronous trip + clean error ordering)

assumptions.context: On overflow, destroy upstream OR end the counter cleanly?
assumptions.choice: Both, in that order. (1) destroy upstream partStream to stop dicer pumping further body bytes; (2) push MultipartPartTooLargeError into the queue (so it's the FIRST item the consumer's NEXT .next() sees); (3) end the counter cleanly via counter.end() so the consumer's CURRENT in-flight drain on `body` resolves naturally. Without step 3, the consumer's `for await (const _chunk of part.body)` rejects with 'Premature close' (because the counter was destroyed mid-drain), and that reject escapes from the parser's body and is caught by the outer for-await of the iterator BEFORE our typed error has a chance to surface — so the user sees 'Premature close' instead of MultipartPartTooLargeError. Order matters.
alternatives_considered: Destroy the counter with the typed error (counter.destroy(MultipartPartTooLargeError)) (rejected — caller's drain rejects with the typed error directly, but that error then propagates through the parser's catch site rather than the iterator's next .next(); the spec's contract is that the iterator surfaces the error, not the parser)
Just push to queue without destroying counter (rejected — the consumer's drain then hangs waiting for end/error; the counter never gets one)
Set a flag and let the next chunk arrival trigger end() (rejected — too racy; the next chunk may not arrive if dicer was the only producer)

assumptions.context: Where to apply cap defaults: validation-time vs listener-time
assumptions.choice: Validation-time. Right after validatePositiveTimeout (which validates the timeouts via the same shape), we resolve `const maxParts = opts.maxParts ?? 10_000;` etc. This locks the values for the operation's duration. The listeners reference the closure-scoped resolved values, NOT opts.* directly.
alternatives_considered: Resolve in the listener (rejected — would re-resolve on every fire and would couple listener correctness to opts.* mutability)
Resolve in a setupCaps() helper (rejected — three lines of `?? DEFAULT` don't justify a function; the validation-time site is the right spot)

assumptions.context: DicerHeaderBag value shape and the `Array.isArray(value) ? value : [value]` normalization
assumptions.choice: Dicer 0.3.1's HeaderParser always emits `Record<string, string[]>` per the existing flatten-headers.ts rationale. The ambient shim documents the broader `Buffer | Buffer[] | Buffer[][]` shape for forward-compat. The Sprint 6 cap code wraps each value in `Array.isArray(value) ? value : [value]` so the iteration shape is uniform, even if a forward-incompatible dicer version ever emits a non-array value (in which case the array branch's else delivers a single-element array — same effect as the array branch with one entry). This trade-off keeps the count semantics consistent across forward-compat shapes.
alternatives_considered: Branch on Array.isArray(value) and handle each shape inline (rejected — duplicates the inner iteration body)
Flatten the bag first and then iterate string keys (rejected — flattenDicerHeaders joins repeats with `, ` per RFC 7230, losing the per-repeat count semantic the cap needs)

assumptions.context: Coverage gate: src/parse-multipart-related.ts dropped from 90.32% (Sprint 5) to 90.8% branch with Sprint 6 changes (still meets ≥90% gate)
assumptions.choice: Initial Sprint 6 implementation drove branch coverage down to 86.51% because the new cap-overflow branches included some defensive paths that dicer never actually exercises (e.g., `Buffer.isBuffer` in measureHeaderValueBytes; the `else if (value !== undefined)` non-array path; the `Array.isArray(value) ? value.length : 1` ternary's else). Remaining uncovered branches are Sprint 3+4 carry-overs (cleaned-after-cleanup race paths) plus a few defensive Buffer-shape paths in measureHeaderValueBytes that dicer 0.3.1 never emits.

Move measureHeaderValueBytes to src/internal/ and unit-test directly (rejected — adds another file; for a 12-line helper the integration coverage via parse-resource-caps.test.ts is sufficient)
Keep the defensive Buffer/string branches and lower the gate (rejected — the spec gate is 90% and we cleared it without dropping the defenses)

assumptions.context: PassThrough vs Transform for the maxPartBytes wrapper
assumptions.choice: PassThrough. node:stream.PassThrough is a Transform with no transformation — it just passes bytes through with internal buffering when downstream isn't reading. Sprint 6 doesn't transform bytes; it counts them via an external listener on the upstream partStream. PassThrough is the canonical idiom. Transform with a `_transform` override would add ceremony for no benefit.
